source: Bossard et al. (2022) NDM in sport: RPD advances (Frontiers in Psychology opinion)
finding: Opinion piece, no new data. Summarises RPD use in sport and lists six untested research avenues.
numbers: Citing Macquet 2020: simple match 60-81% of decisions, diagnosis 13-28%, course-of-action evaluation 3-24%. Expert athletes chose their preferred first option in about 80% of decisions (source not named). 16 cited works over 12 sports.
quote: There is a lack of consistent empirical evidence in a sport setting
limits: No sample sizes. Usage rates come from mostly qualitative interview studies. The 80% figure is unsourced.
agent_relevance: Usage-rate prior for the agent: most expert decisions are simple pattern match, deliberate simulation is the minority. Do not build a schema where simulation runs on every decision.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) moderators of analysis in sport
finding: Time pressure and role moderate how much analysis occurs. Players far from the ball (handball goalkeepers, distant soccer defenders) simulate more. Rugby coaches under less time pressure decide more analytically.
numbers: No numbers given for the moderators. Cites Le Menn 2019, Kermarrec and Bossard 2014, Collins 2016.
limits: Authors say time pressure may not fully explain intuition; role and context also matter. No sport study of emotion effects.
agent_relevance: Scale deliberation to time budget and role, not one fixed depth. An operator could pick pattern match, diagnose or simulate by time available.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) unproven intuition-analysis continuum
finding: The idea that intuition and analysis sit on one continuum, and that intuition develops in a U shape, lacks sport evidence. NDM-based training programmes are rare.
numbers: No effect sizes. Evidence on intuition development described as lacking.
limits: Creativity link weak: first-option findings suggest expert athletes may be non-creative.
agent_relevance: Do not claim RPD-style scaffolds are validated by sport training results. Evidence for trained gains is thin.

source: Ashford, Abraham and Poolton (2021) Understanding a player's decision-making process in team sports: systematic review (Sports)
finding: Narrative systematic review of 53 empirical studies across information-processing, ecological-dynamics and NDM views. Four studies supported RPD levels 1-3; level 3 simulation was rarely verbalised in team sports.
numbers: 53 studies, 2,078 participants (2,021 players, 57 coaches). Perspectives: information processing 25, ecological dynamics 18, NDM 10. No pooled effect sizes, no formal risk-of-bias tool.
limits: Counting inconsistencies in the paper (41 vs 53 studies; 13 vs 7 added). Decontextualised tasks. Mostly visual cues, auditory cues ignored.
agent_relevance: Best large map of the sport evidence, but a narrative review. Treat 'RPD supported' as qualitative support, not a measured effect.

source: Ashford et al. (2021) experts and visual search results are mixed
finding: Experts are more accurate and pick up salient or global cues earlier, but visual-search results conflict between studies.
numbers: Lex et al.: fewer fixations in experts. Roca et al.: more fixations in experts in full 11 v 11 scenes. Kinrade et al. (38 skilled basketball players): decision reinvestment negatively associated with performance on complex tasks.
limits: Sign of the expert fixation effect depends on task complexity and display.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage is about which cues, not how many. For an agent: cue selection beats cue count.

source: Ashford et al. (2021) intuition, less-is-more and first-option results
finding: Time and option count interact. With little time intuitive first responses were more effective; with more time, generating more options helped. Fewer options gave more accurate first responses in a large soccer sample.
numbers: Basevitch: 40 males, high vs low skill soccer. Musculus: 169 male soccer players, supports less-is-more. Raab and Laborde: 54 youth handball players, deliberators less successful than intuitive players. Klatt: Brazilian players more accurate than German and generated more options.
quote: their intuitive responses were more effective when less time was available
limits: Mixed: Klatt result (more options, higher accuracy) conflicts with less-is-more. Culture differs.
agent_relevance: Discriminating condition: extra options pay off only when time allows. Gate option generation by time budget.

source: Collins, Collins and Carson (2016) If it feels right, do it: intuitive decision making in high-level coaches (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Interviews with 18 elite coaches. All recognised intuitive decisions. Most audited a fast decision with a quick check. Intuition was tied to creative solutions.
numbers: N=18 male British coaches (10 adventure sport, 8 rugby union), about 15 years experience. Rugby coaches self-estimated about 30% intuitive (range 5-40%); one adventure coach said about 90%. 8 of 10 adventure and 4 of 8 rugby coaches showed an integrated intuitive plus deliberative meta-process. 7 of 10 adventure and 7 of 8 rugby coaches linked intuition to creativity.
quote: I decide to do something, say make a substitution, but immediately I'm scanning the decision to see if it feels right.
limits: Small, male, British, personal contacts, retrospective self-report. Percentage question was crude. Self-estimates vary from 5% to 90%, so usage rates from self-report are weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Pattern: intuit, then audit. A ready model for a cheap fast answer followed by a short check step.

source: Collins et al. (2016) role of reflection in coach intuition
finding: Sources of intuitive skill differ: adventure coaches used personal reflection and a community; rugby coaches relied on mentors and only 2 of 8 reflected regularly.
numbers: N=18 total; 2 of 8 rugby coaches reported regular self-directed reflection.
limits: Same small interview sample.
agent_relevance: Experience alone is not enough; supports a post-decision review step, not just fast action.

source: Hepler and Feltz (2012) Take the first heuristic, self-efficacy, and decision-making in sport (J Exp Psychol Appl)
finding: Video basketball tasks: people used take-the-first on most trials, earlier options were better than later ones. Higher self-efficacy went with using TTF more and generating fewer options.
numbers: N=72, 13 trials in each of two video basketball tasks. TTF used on 70% of trials. No difference in dynamic inconsistency or confidence by option count.
limits: Abstract only read (via Europe PMC). Participants were students, not elite athletes, so expertise generalisation is limited.
agent_relevance: Replication of TTF outside handball with non-experts. Option quality falls with generation order; the first option is a strong default.

source: Raab and Laborde (2011) When to blink and when to think: preference for intuitive decisions (Res Q Exerc Sport)
finding: Handball players who prefer intuitive decisions made faster and better choices than those classed as deliberative. Experts were more intuitive than near-experts and non-experts.
numbers: N=54 male and female handball players of different expertise levels. Effect sizes not seen in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Lab video task. Preference is a trait measure, so link to training is correlational.
agent_relevance: Individual-differences moderator: style preference matters. A scaffold should not force deliberation where fast matching already works.

source: Raab and Johnson (2007) Expertise-based differences in search and option-generation strategies (J Exp Psychol Appl)
finding: Two-year longitudinal handball study with eye tracking. Athletes of all levels generated the same number of options on average, but option quality differed by expertise for both first and final choices.
numbers: Experts, near-experts, non-experts; sample sizes not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only read. The founder paper (Johnson and Raab 2003) was not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Experts do not search more, they generate better options first. Quality of the first generated option is the lever.

source: Musculus and colleagues (2019) A developmental perspective on option generation and selection (Developmental Psychology)
finding: Children 6-13 in a soccer task generated few options in decreasing validity and chose the first. Older children chose the first more often and generated faster. Time limits gave fewer, better options.
numbers: N=73 children, four measurement waves.
limits: Abstract only. Author list and DOI given from memory of the search listing; check before citing.
agent_relevance: TTF is learned and strengthens with age and a time limit. A time-limited first pass is a legitimate design, not only a shortcut.

source: Klatt and colleagues (2019) Creative and intuitive decision-making: Brazilian and German soccer coaches and players
finding: In real-match video, number of options generated correlated positively with quality of both first and final option, and first option beat later ones. Player creativity score correlated with first-option quality.
numbers: Two studies (coaches, players), two countries. No sample sizes in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Positive options-quality link partly conflicts with less-is-more in the Musculus sample (N=169). DOI from memory; check.
agent_relevance: Failed to converge: whether more options help depends on sample and task. Do not hard-code 'fewer options is better'.

source: Raab and Gigerenzer (2015) The power of simplicity: fast-and-frugal heuristics for performance science (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Perspective that cites take-the-first support in elite handball (Johnson and Raab 2003) and basketball (Hepler and Feltz), plus influence of personality, mood and situation on TTF. Reports no failures to replicate.
numbers: No sample sizes or effect sizes in the paper. Boundary conditions: option validity varies, validity is learned through feedback. Wimbledon 127 matches: recognition heuristic beat ATP rankings and seeding in two studies. A 3-question fast-and-frugal tree for chest pain beat physicians, no numbers given.
limits: Written by TTF proponents; qualitative. No discussion of deliberation-without-attention.
agent_relevance: TTF depends on option validity and feedback learning. In a new domain without feedback the agent should not trust first options.

source: North et al. (2011) via Raab and Gigerenzer (2015): long-term working memory rival to take-the-first
finding: Rival account: long-term working memory predicts that generating more options improves performance. Take-the-first predicts a negative relation between option count and performance.
numbers: Two models, opposite-sign predictions. The citing paper gives no data.
limits: Secondary mention only; North 2011 itself not opened.
agent_relevance: A discriminating test exists: sign of the option-count to performance link. Klatt 2019 (positive) versus Musculus and Hepler (negative) split along it.

source: Option generation in decision making: ideation beyond memory retrieval (Frontiers in Psychology 2014)
finding: Individual-differences study: option fluency and diversity are supported by ideation ability beyond memory retrieval. Generating more options raises best-option quality but lowers mean quality of the set.
numbers: N=141 undergraduates, three ill-structured scenarios. Correlations between option fluency and choice quality all non-significant (for example parking r=-0.01, fund raising r=0.08).
limits: Student sample, non-sport, poorly structured everyday problems.
agent_relevance: Partly resolves the dispute: more options raise the maximum, not the average. Fits sampling many options plus a selector, not a take-the-first rule.

source: Secondary analysis of option generation task design and heuristics (2025)
finding: Culture-free path-drawing task: uniqueness and diversity fell as fluency rose, matching less-is-more and conflicting with quantity-breeds-quality.
numbers: 44 healthy people and 54 people with Major Depressive Disorder, 1.5 minutes per task.
limits: Abstract only. Not sport. The authors say task design steers which heuristic appears to hold.
agent_relevance: Task design decides which option-generation effect you see. Treat sport TTF results as task-bound.

source: Hinz et al. (2022) Elite vs amateur handball decision making in a near-game test (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: With motor responses on a contact plate, elite players chose offensive responses more often, but decision time did not differ by expertise. Decision time fell with more visual information.
numbers: N=44 handball players; elite offensive-response odds ratios 2.76-3.00, p<0.05, left-handed attacks only. No expertise effect on decision time.
limits: Effect only in left-handed sequences. Authors note verbal and micro-movement decisions differ from on-field decisions.
agent_relevance: Expertise shows in what is chosen, not how fast. Speed is a poor proxy for skill when evaluating an agent.

source: Roca, Ford and Memmert (2018) Creative decision making and visual search in skilled soccer players (PLoS ONE)
finding: Most-creative players produced more original, flexible, fluent and appropriate decisions and used a broader attentional focus with more, shorter fixations on informative locations.
numbers: N=44 skilled players, 11 most-creative vs 11 least-creative. Fixation locations per second t(20)=2.15, p=.044, d=0.91.
limits: Extreme-group split with n=11 each, so effect sizes are likely inflated. One lab simulation.
agent_relevance: Creative option generation tied to wide cue sampling. Schema analogue: scan a broad cue set before committing.

source: Powless et al. (2020) Video-based training to improve decision making in high school quarterbacks (Sports)
finding: Computer learning modules using temporal occlusion did not show a causal accuracy gain but gave moderate evidence of faster decisions. The lowest working-memory participant improved most.
numbers: N=4 quarterbacks, single-subject multiple baseline. For one participant improvement rate difference was 60% for accuracy (moderate) and 80% for reaction time (large).
limits: Four participants. Authors say results did not demonstrate a causal accuracy effect.
agent_relevance: Training gained speed without accuracy. Beware optimising latency or confidence instead of correctness when training with scaffold feedback.

source: Decision-making in youth team-sports players: systematic review (2020)
finding: High-level youth players decide more accurately. Practice-scenario training (small-sided games) improved passing decisions. Benefit of video interventions unclear.
numbers: 26 articles from 6,215 records: 9 on skill-level comparisons, 6 on age groups, 11 on training programmes. One handball study: 2-D and 3-D video both improved decision times, 3-D slightly more.
quote: the benefits of interventions using videos are not clear
limits: Narrative review, heterogeneous measures, no pooled effects.
agent_relevance: Interventions that train in-situ choice beat passive video review. Active practice on realistic tasks is the better scaffold analogue.

source: Instructional design for accelerated macrocognitive expertise in the baseball workplace (Frontiers in Psychology 2016)
finding: Part-task perceptual training on pitch recognition in one college team. The team went from sixth of 11 to first in conference in runs scored and batting average, but a comparison team also improved.
numbers: One team, one season. Pitch-recognition test vs batting r=0.53, p=0.052 (11 of 18 batters qualified); test-retest r=0.707, p=0.117.
limits: Single case, no randomisation, comparison team also improved and won the post-season. Correlations not significant.
agent_relevance: Case-level evidence only. Not proof that perception training raises game performance.

source: Effectiveness of a video-feedback and questioning programme to develop cognitive expertise in sport (PLoS ONE 2013)
finding: Ten sessions of video feedback with open questions improved on-court decision accuracy in young tennis players and the richness of tactical knowledge.
numbers: N=11 (experimental 5, control 6). Successful decisions: experimental 55.54% to 61.20%, control 58.65% to 54.95%. Interaction F(1,9)=19.318, p=.002, partial eta squared .682. Post-test difference 6.25 points, 95% CI [-12.0, -0.5].
limits: Tiny sample, non-random groups, no placebo, single coder. Tactical knowledge reported with no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Questioning that makes the performer state conditions, goals and actions raised knowledge. Analogue: force the agent to write cues, goals, expectancies, not just an answer.

source: Kopka and Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomedical Engineering)
finding: Prompts built on recognition-primed decision-making and on data-frame theory raised accuracy on 45 patient vignettes across 10 ChatGPT models. Gains were largest for self-care cases, where models were otherwise too cautious.
numbers: 10 models x 3 prompts x 45 vignettes x 10 repeats. Accuracy: default 63.3%, RPD prompt 67.6%, data-frame 66.7%. Self-care accuracy 13.4% (default) to 29.8% (RPD) and 24.6% (data-frame). Gains in all models except GPT-5.2. The 2 emergency and 30 nonemergency cases stayed high.
quote: NDM concepts have not yet been applied to LLM prompt engineering.
limits: One domain, one benchmark; only 2 emergency cases so no safety claim; only ChatGPT models; extra tokens cost more; no human users; no sport task.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of RPD prompting: about +4 points overall, mostly by unlocking a rarely chosen class. Use an RPD recall-then-simulate step but expect modest gains and test per model.

source: Kopka and Feufel (2026) reasoning-model comparison
finding: RPD and data-frame prompts helped reasoning models too, so the gain is not only from extra reasoning text. Non-reasoning models with NDM prompts mostly beat reasoning models on the default prompt. Non-reasoning models reached up to 44% self-care accuracy.
numbers: Same design as above; non-reasoning models began giving self-care advice they gave rarely or never by default.
limits: No ablation separating 'recall similar cases' from 'simulate outcomes'. Authors say the gain may partly reflect added reasoning.
agent_relevance: Supports cheap NDM scaffolds on non-reasoning backbones. The missing ablation suggests testing each step alone.

source: Scoping review of generative AI and LLMs in sports medicine (Frontiers in Public Health 2026)
finding: Searched 2022 to March 2026. Applications are training, nutrition, rehab, mental health, clinical support and writing; the abstract lists no study of LLM game-tactics decisions.
numbers: 1,847 records, 32 included (training 5, nutrition 4, rehabilitation 3, mental health 3, clinical decision support 5, writing 6, ethics 6). Sleep advice validity ratio 0.33 (GPT-3.5) vs 0.67 (GPT-4). AI text in sports medicine journals 2.38% to 6.25%.
limits: Abstract only. Sports medicine, not game decisions. Authors cite a lack of sport-specific validation datasets.
agent_relevance: Gap: no LLM benchmark of RPD in athletic play found in my limited search. Absence from a limited search is not proof.

source: NeuroPlayNet (2026) multimodal AI framework for basketball strategy (Scientific Reports)
finding: Neuro-symbolic reinforcement-learning system reports gains over baselines in simulated NBA environments. Not an LLM and not a test of RPD.
numbers: Shot success prediction +12.6%, injury risk -18.9% with fatigue-aware substitution timing, win probability forecasting +9.4%. Simulated games enriched with broadcast data.
limits: Abstract only. Simulation, no human expert comparison.
agent_relevance: Not evidence for or against RPD. Listed so it is not mistaken for a test of NDM.

source: Ashford et al. (2021) paradigm bias as a boundary condition
finding: Review authors say the theory used drives the method used, and some ecological studies assumed no mental representations, showing confirmation bias.
numbers: No numbers. Ecological dynamics 18 of 53 studies.
limits: Interpretive claim of the review authors.
agent_relevance: Rival theory (ecological dynamics) is not refuted by the RPD evidence. Do not state RPD as settled.

source: Bossard et al. (2022) creativity and first-option link as indirect evidence
finding: The positive correlation between creativity and first-option quality in real soccer footage is described as indirect evidence, because those studies were not about RPD processes.
numbers: No coefficients or N reported in the opinion article.
quote: Even if the topics of those studies were not the recognition primed-decision processes.
limits: Indirect support only.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. First-option quality relates to option generation, not recognition matching.
